body.text: Americans try and succeed at looking their best (other than the poor, and the mass of President Donald Trump’s unwashed voter base). Americans wear the best clothes; they have the best skin; their hair is forever washed and processed; and they eat steak. Each remains, however, The Ugly American, the title of Eugene Burdick and William Lederer’s 1958 novel.

Their novel drew inspiration from Graham Greene’s prescient The Quiet American, a 1955 novel whose hero, Alden Pyle, an undercover CIA agent, represents growing American involvement (as the colonial French draw down) in Vietnam. He is so blinded by “American exceptionalism” that he cannot see the calamities he is bringing upon the country.

American exceptionalism refers to that nation’s self-belief that it is different from other nations, which gives it a unique historical and political role on the global stage. Its roots go back to the 1630s, when New England was settled by Puritans who believed that God had chosen them for the New World to establish “a city on the hill”. America’s 1776 revolution was based on universal principles of rights and equality, and laid a framework for a transcendental, or Platonic, ideal of governance.

Alexis de Tocqueville visited the US in 1831, and in his famous Democracy in America he first used the word “exceptional”. In 1929, Joseph Stalin, the general secretary of the USSR (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics), called it “the heresy of American exceptionalism”. President Ronald Reagan, who marshalled US power to defeat the USSR, called his society the “shining city on the hill”. It was this self-image that Greene derided, correctly predicting that America would have its first debacle in Vietnam.

In The Ugly American, a fictional South-East Asian country (but obviously Vietnam), a plain-looking Homer Atkins lives among the locals and tries to help them with small-scale projects. He witnesses the bungling of the US diplomatic corps, which is arrogant and has little time to understand the local culture. U Maung Swe, a Burmese journalist, says: “For some reason, the [American] people I meet in my country are not the same as the ones I knew in the United States. A mysterious change seems to come over Americans when they go to a foreign land. They isolate themselves socially. They live pretentiously. They are loud and ostentatious.”

It is the same today, be it President Donald Trump’s men in West Asia, in Europe, in East Asia, or even in India, for that matter. Were it not so, America would not find itself having lost a war in Iran this year, despite superior weaponry that is technologically light years ahead of what any other country has, including China; it would not have launched an economic D-Day against Iran, trying to invoke the famous 1944 Normandy beach landings in France by Allied Forces to defeat Germany’s Third Reich. (Incidentally, the Nazis were defeated by the USSR, an Allied power that lost 27 million people in the Second World War, and not by the Americans, who even now claim that were it not for them, the British would now be speaking in Deutsche.)

So stale was Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement that not even Americans took him seriously. China told America where to get off, and now America has proposed to cancel “Operation Economic Outcast”, if Iran opens the Strait of Hormuz. Iran is not budging from its position.

American exceptionalism in its latest avatar is not an idea, an ideal, or an ideology; it is a vanity. No wonder that Trump the narcissist, became President. His ridiculous blonde comb-over is common among octogenarians. His suits might be the finest in American tailoring, though he wears his tie too low, but it cannot cover the alleged stench from his geriatric diaper, as many press photos at public events attest to, with attendees reflexively holding their noses.

America is no longer an ideal of democracy: its legislature is a rubber stamp, and even its Supreme Court, as craven as our own, has allowed Trump to manipulate the mail-in voting system ahead of the midterm polls, that is expected to sweep the Democrats into controlling the legislative branch of government, thereby ending Trump’s run of absolute power. Currently, America is not even an exceptional banana republic.

In the two months that I spent in the US, I occasionally watched televised sports, which feature games that are unique to America, so that it may dominate that game: like baseball or American football. Sports have become a corporate caricature of what they were 50 years ago. Players have no allegiance to their cities or fans, only to their eight-figure salaries. The worst seat costs $65; a beer costs $16. Even the World Cup was sought to be monetised and was nearly captured by a consortium controlled by Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The venality and greed of the Trump crime family is not exceptional, however; all over the world, strongmen are using power not to benefit their nations economically, but themselves.

Nothing can save America, not even the Democratic Socialists; already the likely next Speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries, is holding secret meetings with Kushner and has placed a pro-war, pro-Israel Democratic hawk, Jared Moskowitz, as the ranking member on the Congressional Foreign Affairs Subcommittee for the Middle East and North Africa; his job will be to disallow any investigation into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, when the Democrats take power. It shows that, if anything, the corrupt structure of American power and elitism remains exceptionally intact. The free fall of American decline will continue.

America might look attractive on the surface, with its stylishly coiffured white men and women, armed with Botox and liposuction; fed well (like Napoleon’s fellow pigs in Orwell’s Animal Farm) while the rest of the population eats over-processed, toxic food; wearing the finest-textured clothes; driving an endless variety of cars; and living a life of luxury vacations. Yet underneath the sparkle there is a relentless rot. American exceptionalism is dead; long live the Ugly American.
Aditya Sinha is a writer living on the outskirts of Delhi.
